intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 8 units · tectonics to contours

Grade 12 is “geography of Eritrea in depth”. Grade 11 is the toolkit: how the crust moves, how water and wind carve, how people settle, then a first look at Eritrea’s place, relief and contour maps. Read each unit as a *story with a cause* — examiners mark the cause, not only the landform name.

units.title: Map Work: Landforms on Contour Maps
units.intro:
A **contour line** joins every point that is the same height above a datum (usually sea level). The map does not show every metre — it samples at a fixed **contour interval** (e.g. 20 m). Read the printed numbers; never guess the interval.

**Spacing is slope.** Packed lines = you climb a lot in a short walk = steep (escarpment). Wide lines = gentle (western plains). A uniform spacing = even slope. Lines that suddenly pack after being wide = a break of slope (terrace edge, cliff).

f3.title: Gradient = rise / horizontal distance (same units). Cross-section: walk a line across the map and plot heights. Intervis

cards.title: 8.1 Major Land forms on Maps
body: Hill: A hill is an area of land usually rounded in shape that is higher than the surrounding areas.
A hill has a broad base and is almost circular in shape.
Contours showing a conical hill are almost circular with peak of the hill at their center.
Contour lines representing a hill are drawn almost at regular distances.
The value of contour increases towards the centre.

cards.title: Reading contours
body: A **contour** joins points of equal height above sea level. The **contour interval** is the height difference between neighbouring contours. **Close** contours = steep slope; **wide** (far apart) contours = gentle slope; evenly spaced contours = uniform slope. Contours never cross each other (except at an overhanging cliff).

cards.title: Major landforms and how contours show them
body: **Hill:** rounded land higher than its surroundings, broad base and narrow top. Contours are roughly circular and evenly spaced, with values **increasing towards the centre**. A conical hill rises about 300 m above its surroundings. A **volcanic hill** looks the same but has a **crater** (a ring of lower contour) at the summit.
**Mountain:** larger and higher than a hill (over about 600 m above its surroundings), with a small summit area. Contours are closed rings, closely spaced on steep sides.

**Mountain ridge:** a long, narrow stretch of high ground with a series of peaks separated by lower sections (saddles, cols). Contours are **elongated and close together**. The steeper side is the **scarp slope**; the gentler side is the **dip slope**.
**Plateau:** high land with a broad, nearly level top and steep edges (escarpments). Contours are **crowded at the sides** and almost **absent in the middle**.

cards.title: Identify a landform from contour patterns
cards.problem: On a map, a set of closed contours is crowded together at the edges, but the large central area inside the highest contour (2,400 m) has no other contours. Name the landform and explain how you know.

steps.text: **Step 1: Closed contours with the highest value inside** = high ground.
**Step 2: Crowded contours at the edges** = steep sides (escarpments).
**Step 3: Wide area with no contours inside** = almost level top.
**Step 4: Match.** High, steep-sided and flat-topped = a plateau (a hill or mountain would have a small summit).

cards.answer: A plateau: closed contours rising inwards, crowded at the steep edges and absent over the wide flat top.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: On a contour map, closely spaced contours on the sides and almost none in the middle of a high area show a ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Close contours mean steep slopes; no contours mean nearly level ground.

**Step 2:** High ground with steep sides and a flat top is a plateau.

**Step 3:** A conical hill has evenly spaced rings up to a small peak.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The gentler slope of a mountain ridge is called the ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** A ridge has two sides with different steepness.

**Step 2:** The steeper side is the scarp slope; the gentler side is the dip slope.

**Step 3:** A crater is a hollow and a saddle is a low point between peaks.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A volcanic hill differs from a conical hill because it has ____.

options.B: a flat top many kilometres wide

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Both are roughly circular with contours rising towards the top.

**Step 2:** A volcanic hill has a hollow (crater) at the summit, shown by a lower contour inside the highest ring.

**Step 3:** A wide flat top describes a plateau.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: 8.2 Minor Land forms on Maps
body: A single type of a major land form may contain one or more types of minor land forms.
A mountain ridge, for example, may include many other minor land features. due to external and internal forces.
Valley: A valley is a depressed area formed either by tectonic forces or the agents of weathering.
Depending on the nature and magnitude of such natural forces, valleys can attain either a V or a U-shaped pattern.
A V-shaped valley is formed by the erosion of a river.

cards.title: Minor Land forms on Maps
body: **Closed loop** with values rising toward the centre = hill or mountain. Closed loop with values falling toward the centre (sometimes marked with hachure ticks) = hollow or crater. Two loops sharing a saddle = col / pass — the usual road place across a ridge.

cards.title: Recognising landforms
body: Hill: closed rings rising inward. **Spur:** V or U shaped contours pointing **downhill**. **Valley:** V shaped contours pointing **uphill** (upstream). Plateau: high flat top with contours spaced widely in the middle and close together at the edges. **Saddle:** a low area between two hills. **Cliff:** contours very close together or merging. **Gorge:** very close contours on both sides of a narrow valley.

cards.title: Valleys, spurs, saddles, passes and cols
body: **V-shaped valley:** narrow and deep, cut by a river. Contours form a V whose **point aims upstream** (towards higher ground); the river runs through the V.
**U-shaped valley:** flat floor and steep sides, carved by a glacier. Steep sides = closely spaced U-shaped contours; the flat floor has almost no contours.
**Spur:** a tongue of high land sticking out into lower ground. Its contours also form a V, but the **V points downhill** (towards lower ground). Valleys and spurs usually alternate along a hillside.

**Saddle:** a low area between two hills, only slightly lower than them; it does not form a route through the mountains. **Pass:** a lower gap between two mountain peaks that does provide a route. **Col:** a term used for a pass or saddle across a ridge.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: On a contour map, point **K** lies where the contours form a V shape pointing towards **lower** ground. Point K is on a:
cards.why: Contours that form a V pointing towards lower ground show a tongue of high land sticking out into lower land. That is a **spur**. (A valley's V points the other way, towards higher ground.)

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: On a contour map, point **T** lies at a low point on the crest between two hilltops, only slightly lower than both. Point T is on a:
cards.why: A low area between two higher hilltops, only slightly lower than them, is a **saddle** (col). A pass is a lower gap that provides a route through mountains.

cards.title: Intervisibility
body: **Valley vs spur.** Contours bend into a V. If the V points *upslope* (into the highland), you are looking at a valley — water runs out of the V. If the V points *downslope*, it is a spur standing out from the hill. Rivers are drawn along the valley V, never along the spur V.
**Gradient** = vertical rise ÷ horizontal distance (same units). Example: 100 m rise over 2 000 m run = 1/20 or 5%. On the map, measure the run with the scale; read the rise from contour numbers.
**Cross-section:** lay a paper edge on the map line, tick every contour with its height, transfer the ticks to graph paper, join the dots. That drawing is what “the land looks like along A–B.”

**Intervisibility:** can a person at A see a person at B? Draw the A–B section. If any ridge rises above the straight line of sight, they cannot see each other. Trees and buildings also block, but the textbook wants the landform reason first.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: On a contour map, V-shaped contours pointing towards higher ground show a ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** In a valley the contours bend upstream, so the V points to higher ground.

**Step 2:** A spur's V points to lower ground.

**Step 3:** Plateaus and hilltops are shown by closed contours.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: 8.3 Gradients and Cross Sections
body: Gradient expresses the ratio of change in the altitude of a slope.
In other words, it expresses the ratio between vertical distance and horizontal distance.
The measurement of a gradient is used for the purpose of comparing the steepness of slopes more accurately.
To calculate the gradient between any two points on a contour map, two things must be known.
Knowledge of a gradient becomes very useful in the construction of roads and railways in mountainous areas.

cards.title: Gradient formula
head: Term
Meaning
rows: Difference in height between two points
Ground distance between them (from the map scale)
VI ÷ HE, written as 1 : n (same units)

cards.title: Calculating and using gradients
body: **Gradient** compares the vertical distance (difference in height, VI) with the horizontal distance (ground distance from the map scale, HE). Always use the same units.
It can be written as a **ratio** (VI : HE, e.g. 1 in 10), a **percentage** (VI ÷ HE × 100, e.g. 10%) or in **degrees** (the angle of slope; a 1 in 10 slope is about 6°).
Example: A at 1,300 m, B at 1,000 m, 4 cm apart on a map where 1 cm = 500 m. VI = 300 m; HE = 4 × 500 = 2,000 m; gradient = 300 : 2,000 = 1 in 6.7 ≈ 15%.

Gradients matter for transport: a train can climb only about **1 in 50 (2%)**, a bicycle about 1 in 20 (5%) and an ordinary car about 1 in 5 (20%). That is why the Massawa–Asmara road (about 115 km) and railway zigzag up the escarpment instead of taking the direct 70 km.

cards.title: Worked example: gradient
cards.problem: Point A is at 1,800 m and point B at 2,000 m. On a 1:50,000 map they are 8 cm apart. Find the gradient.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Point A is at 1,300 m and point B at 1,000 m. They are 4 cm apart on a map where 1 cm represents 500 m. What is the average gradient from A to B?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Vertical interval = 1,300 − 1,000 = 300 m.

**Step 2:** Horizontal distance = 4 × 500 = 2,000 m.

**Step 3:** Gradient = 300 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 15%.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why do the road and railway from Massawa to Asmara climb the escarpment in zigzags?

options.C: To reduce the gradient so vehicles and trains can climb

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The escarpment is very steep.

**Step 2:** Zigzags make the route longer but the slope gentler.

**Step 3:** Trains need gradients of about 2% or less, so the railway zigzags even more than the road.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The average gradient between two points is 1 in 25. What is it as a percentage?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Gradient % = vertical ÷ horizontal × 100.

**Step 2:** 1 ÷ 25 × 100 = 4%.

**Step 3:** 4% is too steep for a train (about 2% limit) but easy for a car.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: 8.4 Intervisibility
body: Two points A and B on the ground are said to be intervisible if point A can be seen from point B and point B can be seen from point A.

cards.title: Gradient = rise / horizontal distance (same units). Cross-section: walk a line across the map and plot heights. Intervisibility: can A see B? Draw the section — a ridge in the way blocks the view.
Tricks that save marks
body: 1) V into the hill = valley. 2) Count the interval before you shout “steep”. 3) Gradient needs both rise and scale distance — height marks alone are not a gradient. 4) Intervisibility without a section is a guess.

cards.title: Revision checklist (say these out loud)
body: - Packed contours = steep. V into the hill = valley. Gradient = rise / run. Intervisibility needs a section.

cards.title: Decide whether two points are intervisible
cards.problem: Point P is at 1,200 m and point Q at 1,150 m. On the straight line between them the ground rises to 1,260 m. Can a person at P see Q?

steps.text: **Step 1: Rule.** Two points are intervisible only if no ground between them is higher than the line joining them.
**Step 2: Compare heights.** The ground between them reaches 1,260 m, higher than both P (1,200 m) and Q (1,150 m).
**Step 3: Decide.** The high ground (a convex slope or ridge) blocks the line of sight.
**Step 4: Check method.** On a real map, draw a cross-section from P to Q and join the two points with a ruler; if the section rises above the line, they are not intervisible.

cards.answer: No – the ground between them (1,260 m) is higher than both points, so it blocks the view.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which pair of points on a contour map is most likely to be **intervisible**?

options.A: P (900 m) and M (700 m) on one smooth concave slope with no higher ground between them
options.B: X (600 m) and Y (650 m) with a 700 m ridge between them
options.C: K and L on opposite sides of a hill summit
options.D: two points in neighbouring valleys separated by a spur

cards.why:
Two points are intervisible only if no ground between them rises above the line joining them.
- **P and M** lie on one concave slope with nothing higher in between, so they can see each other.
- In the other pairs a ridge, summit or spur blocks the line of sight.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Two points are NOT intervisible when ____.

options.A: the slope between them is concave
options.B: both are on the same smooth concave slope
options.C: the slope between them is convex and rises above the line of sight
options.D: nothing between them is higher than the two points

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A convex slope bulges outward and can hide one point from the other.

**Step 2:** A concave slope curves inward, so the points can see each other.

**Step 3:** If no ground is higher than the line joining them, they are intervisible.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The best way to prove intervisibility between two points on a contour map is to ____.

options.B: look at the map key only
options.C: measure the area of the map

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A cross-section shows the actual shape of the ground between the points.

**Step 2:** A straight line joining the two points on the section shows whether any ground blocks it.

**Step 3:** The other methods do not show the profile of the land.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

glossary.meaning: A tongue of high land projecting into lower ground; contours form a V or U pointing downhill.
A low area or dip between two hills on a ridge.
A conical hill is a cone shaped land features and it rises about 300 meters above the surrounding areas.
A long, narrow stretch of high ground.
A large, steep landform rising high above the surrounding land, usually above about 600 m.

tips.text: Geographers use different measurement techniques to classify the morphology or shape of the earth’s physical features.
Elevation, slope steepness are some of the common examples frequently used to classify land forms.
Others may apply only size as major distinguishing criterion. In this unit, the criteria used to identify land features are many.
In this measurement system, some land forms stand out distinctively from their surroundings, while other may be identified in association to distinct land forms.
Land forms that are widely distributed in many places are called major land forms.
Land forms whose presences are mostly linked with the major land forms are called minor land features.
Contour lines representing such land forms show different characteristics.

questions.q: On a contour map with a 100 m interval, point E lies inside three closed loops that are themselves inside the 1600 m contour; points C, H and P lie inside only one or two closed loops inside the same contour, and G lies on a saddle between two hills. Which point is highest?
why: Each closed loop inside the 1600 m contour adds one interval (100 m). E is inside three more loops, so it is above 1900 m (1700, 1800, 1900).
C, H and P have fewer loops, so they are lower hills; a saddle (G) is a low point between two hills.
Answer: B (E).
